notes.h: Biological functions of sugars and starch
notes.b: Carbohydrate is the body's main and quickest source of energy. Sugars and starch both end up as glucose in the body, and what the body does with that glucose explains each of the functions below.
points: Heat and energy: glucose is oxidised in the cells (respiration, the process by which cells release energy from glucose using oxygen). This releases energy for movement and growth and heat to keep body temperature at about 37 °C.
The brain and nervous system rely on glucose as their main fuel, and red blood cells depend on it too, so the body needs a steady supply.
Protein sparing: when enough carbohydrate is eaten to supply energy, protein is kept for growth and repair rather than being used as fuel.
Glycogen store: glucose not needed at once is converted to glycogen and stored in the liver and muscles as a short-term energy reserve, which can be turned back into glucose when blood glucose falls.

Fat store: when the glycogen stores are full, surplus glucose is converted to fat and stored as adipose tissue (body fat) under the skin and around organs, where it also insulates the body and protects organs. Excess energy of any kind is stored this way.
Starch is digested to glucose in the body, so it provides the same energy as sugars, but more slowly.
Sugars give a quick supply of energy. Starch gives a slower, steadier release, along with other nutrients, in foods such as cereals and potatoes.
notes.tip: Give each function with its reason in a short clause: energy and heat, protein sparing, glycogen in the liver and muscles (not one of them alone), then fat only when glycogen stores are full. Do not present carbohydrate as something that is mainly turned into fat.

notes.b: Dietary fibre (non-starch polysaccharide, mainly cellulose) cannot be digested by humans, so it passes through the digestive system. Its value lies in what it does on the way through the bowel.
points: Fibre absorbs water and adds bulk and softness to the contents of the intestine and to the stool, so waste is easier to pass.
The bulk stimulates peristalsis, the wave-like muscular contraction that moves food and waste through the intestine. Waste leaves faster, so there is less time for toxins to form in the bowel.
Regular movement of the bowel prevents constipation and reduces the straining that causes haemorrhoids (piles, swollen veins at the anus).

Low fibre intake is a risk factor for constipation, haemorrhoids, diverticular disease (small pouches forming in the bowel wall, which can become inflamed, called diverticulitis) and colon (bowel) cancer.
Fibre absorbs water and gives a feeling of fullness, which helps control appetite and body weight.
Soluble fibre, such as pectin and the soluble fibre in oats, beans and lentils, slows the release of glucose into the blood, which helps keep blood sugar steady.
Soluble fibre also helps to lower LDL cholesterol (the type of blood cholesterol that raises the risk of heart disease), so it reduces the risk of heart disease.

There are two kinds. Insoluble fibre (cellulose, wheat bran) speeds the movement of waste. Soluble fibre (pectin) slows sugar absorption and lowers LDL cholesterol. Fibre provides little or no usable energy.
notes.tip: For benefits of a high-fibre diet, give each benefit with its reason: slower glucose release, lower LDL cholesterol and heart disease risk, bulk and fullness, faster peristalsis, fewer bowel disorders and lower bowel cancer risk. Say soluble fibre lowers LDL cholesterol, not that it removes cholesterol, and do not say fibre gives energy.

notes.h: Bowel conditions linked to low fibre
notes.b: A diet low in fibre and fluid slows the movement of waste through the bowel. Examiners ask for one bowel disease with an account and its symptoms, and constipation is the model answer.
points: Constipation: stools pass too slowly through the large intestine, so they become hard and difficult to pass, causing discomfort and straining.
Cause: a diet low in fibre and too little water, because without bulk and moisture the stool stays hard and peristalsis is weak.
Effects: hard stools, straining, bloating and discomfort, and a risk of haemorrhoids (piles) from the straining.
Prevention: eat more fibre, drink plenty of fluids and take regular exercise.
Haemorrhoids (piles) and diverticular disease are the other bowel conditions to name if asked, and both are linked to low fibre intake.
Bowel-protecting guidelines: choose wholegrain cereals, leave the skins on fruit and vegetables, snack on fresh or dried fruit, nuts and seeds, eat whole fruit rather than juice, and drink water.
notes.tip: If asked for one bowel disease with account and symptoms, use constipation and give cause, effects and prevention. For guidelines to prevent bowel disease, list practical food choices such as wholegrain cereals, skins on fruit and vegetables, whole fruit rather than juice, and water.

notes.b: Sugar does far more in the kitchen than sweeten. Each use below is something sugar does for the food, and exams ask for three or more.
points: Sweetening and flavouring cakes, desserts, drinks, sauces and sweets, which improves palatability (how pleasant the food is to eat).
Preserving jam, chutney, syrup and crystallised fruit: sugar in high concentration draws water out of micro-organisms, so spoilage is slowed.
Feeding yeast: fermentation of sugar by yeast produces carbon dioxide, which makes bread dough rise.
Browning and caramel flavour: caramelisation and the Maillard reaction brown the surface of baked goods, glazes and crème caramel.
Giving the texture of fudge, fondant and boiled sweets through controlled crystallisation, since sugar crystals form their structure.
Giving volume: creamed sugar and fat trap air in sponge cakes, and sugar helps egg white hold a stable foam in meringues.
Coating: syrups and icing (a solution of sugar) are used for coating, and sugar syrup stops cut fruit in a fruit salad discolouring.
Sugar holds moisture (it is hygroscopic), so cakes stay moist and keep for longer.
notes.tip: To list uses of sugar, choose clear ones such as sweetener, preservative, glaze or colour, aerating, yeast food, icing and syrup. Give each use with what it does for the food.

notes.h: Culinary functions of starch and pectin
notes.b: Starch and pectin are carbohydrates that change how food holds together. Starch mainly thickens, while pectin sets fruit into a gel.
points: Starch is a thickening agent: it gelatinises (swells and thickens) in a hot liquid, thickening sauces, soups, gravies, custards and pie fillings.
In a roux the fat binds with the flour and separates the starch granules, so the sauce is lump-free.
Starch binds and coats: it forms the thickening in batters and coatings and gives body to a sauce.

Starch helps structure in baking: starch in flour gelatinises as a cake, pastry or bread bakes and helps to set the crumb. The elastic structure of bread comes from gluten, a protein in wheat flour, not from starch.
Starch browns on dry heat (dextrinisation), giving crust colour and flavour to toast and baked goods.
Pectin is the gelling agent in jam, jelly and marmalade: with sugar and acid it sets the fruit mixture into a gel.
Pectin is also used in food manufacture as a gelling agent and stabiliser (additive E440) in confectionery, desserts and yoghurts, and it supports shape in cooked fruit and thickens fruit fillings.
notes.tip: For one use of starch, say it is a thickening agent in sauce making. Do not credit starch with the elastic structure of bread or batters, which comes from gluten.

keyTerms.definition: The wave-like contraction of the intestinal muscles that moves food along the digestive tract.
The reserve of glycogen kept in the liver and muscles, which can be converted back to glucose for energy.
The use of carbohydrate for energy so that protein is available for growth and repair.
Body fat stored under the skin and around organs, which stores energy and insulates the body.
Fibre that dissolves or swells in water, such as pectin, which slows the absorption of glucose.
An ingredient, such as pectin, that forms a gel and gives a food its set.
How pleasant a food is to taste and eat, which sugar improves.

factCards.term: Three functions of carbohydrate in the body
factCards.definition: Providing heat and energy, sparing protein, and storing energy as glycogen or adipose tissue.

factCards.term: Four ways fibre helps the bowel
factCards.definition: It absorbs water, adds bulk, stimulates peristalsis and prevents constipation.

factCards.term: Two ways fibre helps control appetite
factCards.definition: It gives a feeling of fullness, and it slows the release of glucose into the blood.

factCards.term: Four conditions linked to low fibre intake
factCards.definition: Constipation, haemorrhoids, diverticular disease and colon cancer.
Setting jam and jelly, and acting as a gelling agent in some confectionery and desserts.

questions.prompt: Outline two ways in which dietary fibre supports the health of the bowel.
questions.model: Fibre absorbs water and adds bulk to the intestinal contents. The bulk stimulates peristalsis, moving food through the intestine. Together these prevent constipation and reduce the straining that causes haemorrhoids, and they lower the risk of diverticular disease.

questions.prompt: Explain the functions of carbohydrates in the body, referring to energy, protein sparing and storage, and the functions of starch and pectin in cooking.
questions.model: Energy: glucose is oxidised in respiration to release heat and energy for movement and growth; the brain depends on glucose. Protein sparing: carbohydrate supplies energy, so protein is kept for growth and repair. Storage: surplus glucose is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles, and excess beyond that is converted to fat stored as adipose tissue, which insulates the body. Fibre: absorbs water, adds bulk, stimulates peristalsis, prevents constipation, gives fullness and slows glucose release. Cooking: starch thickens sauces and soups, binds a roux and gives structure to pastry and bread; pectin sets jam and acts as a gelling agent in desserts.
